documents.title: Backpressure in a Telemetry Pipeline: What Happens When the Cache Falls Behind?

sections.text: I wanted to update a cache as device readings passed through an existing telemetry pipeline. The processor would still publish its events; the cache would keep the latest readings ready for queries. A slow cache, however, would leave the processor with updates waiting to be written. I needed a limit on that work and a decision about what to lose when the limit was reached. The design keeps a bounded set of pending updates, allowing a newer reading to replace an older one for the same device and metric. Revisiting the implementation showed how much depends on what happens after that replacement: which value a writer receives, which write finishes last, and whether a lost reading ever gets another chance. 1 When a consumer cannot keep up 1.1 A queue buys time 1.2 Where the pressure goes 2 A bounded write path for current readings 2.1 Coalesce by device and metric 2.2 Writers must consume the state being coalesced 2.3 Bound everything that retains work 2.4 Preserve ordering at the final write 2.5 A dropped final update does not repair itself 2.6 What I give up, and where the design stops working 3 How I would evolve the system 3.1 Start with the freshness readers need 3.2 Give repair a budget 3.3 Scale the constrained part

sections.heading: 1 When a consumer cannot keep up
sections.text: In From Time-Series to State, I described keeping the latest known device readings in a cache so that queries would not have to reconstruct them from history. That moves work from readers to the ingestion path. Now a processor that already enriches and publishes events also has to maintain the cache. I did not want cache writes to hold up event publication. Pranshu Raj's Backpressure in Distributed Systems discusses the choices available when producers outpace consumers, including slowing producers and dropping work. The cache gives me room to discard some updates; the event log has a different delivery requirement.

sections.heading: 1.1 A queue buys time
sections.text: Suppose a consumer completes 80 updates per second while 100 arrive. With room for 200 updates, an empty queue fills in about ten seconds. These illustrative numbers assume constant rates and equal-cost updates: capacity divided by the excess arrival rate gives us the time until the queue fills. A larger queue absorbs a longer burst. If overload continues, it also makes accepted work wait longer before the queue fills anyway. Launching a goroutine for each blocked send leaves the waiting events in memory, now attached to goroutines. To stay within a memory budget, the system eventually has to accept less work, complete it faster, or discard some of it.

sections.heading: 1.2 Where the pressure goes
sections.text: I use backpressure for feedback that limits what an upstream stage submits. A blocking channel can provide that feedback locally. An asynchronous consumer can advertise demand or stop requesting more work, as in the Reactive Streams model. The submitting thread need not block for the flow of work to slow down. Rejecting an update without slowing its producer is load shedding. Replacing several pending updates with one is coalescing. These protect the consumer without necessarily changing the arrival rate. My cache design relies on both, so calling the whole mechanism backpressure would leave out an important part of its behavior: ingestion can continue while cache updates are lost. When required event processing slows down, a durable log can retain the backlog. Lag still grows, downstream views become stale, and retention is finite. The cache is an optional projection, so I can discard work there to preserve capacity for publication. I can make that trade-off because a newer temperature observation supersedes an older one in the current-state view. It would be wrong for an increment in a consumption total or for an alarm transition or billing event: losing one could change the answer. Even when coalescing is appropriate for a view, historical events may still need to be retained elsewhere.

sections.heading: 2 A bounded write path for current readings
sections.text: My proposal gives the processor a secondary, best-effort path to the current-state cache. It offers each processed measurement to a bounded buffer and continues without waiting for cache I/O. Writers take work from the buffer in batches. If they fall behind, pending updates can be discarded while publication continues. Both paths still share the processor's CPU and memory. The cache branch needs a resource budget even though it does not wait for I/O on the primary path. Figure 1: The intended separation of responsibilities. Cache admission may coalesce or shed updates; required publication needs its own bounded, acknowledged path. The cache branch is a design, not a guarantee of delivery.

sections.heading: 2.1 Coalesce by device and metric
sections.text: A device reports different metrics independently. Replacing a pending temperature update must not remove its pending voltage reading, so the queue's identity is the pair (device, metric). The proposed ring buffer has a fixed number of slots and an index mapping each identity to its slot. A newer observation for an existing identity replaces the pending value in place. An older observation is ignored. When a new identity arrives at capacity, the queue evicts its oldest pending entry. Consider a queue with these pending entries: Device Metric Observation time Value A temperature 10:00:00 21.4 C A voltage 10:00:01 3.5 V B temperature 10:00:02 19.8 C If A/temperature arrives with time 10:00:03, it replaces the first value. The queue still has three pending identities, and the writer can skip the superseded temperature reading. The index avoids scanning for it: lookups are expected O(1), while ring insertion and eviction are O(1). In-place replacement leaves the slot where it was. "Oldest" then means the earliest admitted pending identity, even if its value has just changed. Moving every replacement to the back would change how frequently reporting metrics are evicted. Either policy is possible, but they give different results.

sections.heading: 2.2 Writers must consume the state being coalesced
sections.text: Revisiting the implementation exposed a gap in this design. It keeps recent observations in a ring and sends copies to a separate bounded channel. Writers receive those copies. Replacing a ring entry leaves an older copy already in the channel untouched. If the channel rejects the newer copy, nothing arranges another attempt to deliver the value still held in the ring. Suppose the device stops reporting at that point. The ring holds its newest reading, but the writer may never see it. The ring is acting as a recent-value registry with best-effort notifications, while the proposal needs it to be the queue of pending work. I would have writers claim entries directly from that queue. A channel can wake a writer when work arrives without carrying another set of event copies. The following pseudocode sketches the change; these operations would still need to be implemented: Admission and claiming share one synchronization boundary; network writes happen outside it. offer(event): # while holding the queue lock reject if admission is closed key = (event.device, event.metric) if key is pending: replace only if event.version is newer else: evict oldest pending entry if at capacity insert key and event signal work available claim_batch(limit): # while holding the same lock remove up to limit pending entries remove their index entries return immutable snapshots for the writer Once a writer claims an entry, a newer observation for that metric can become pending again while the earlier write is in flight. If that write fails, its cleanup must leave the newer pending entry alone. Wake-ups may be combined, provided a worker checks the queue before sleeping and cannot miss the transition from empty to nonempty. Admission can briefly wait for the lock protecting the ring and index. "Nonblocking" here means that it does not wait for queue capacity or cache I/O. The writer also needs to copy the claimed event under that lock, before another producer can change its contents. Figure 2: Proposed admission and writer control flow. The queue and index share a mutex; cache writes happen after claiming and unlocking. Slow writes reduce the drain rate, so admission eventually evicts pending work rather than waiting for cache capacity. This is bounded overload control, not producer throttling. The version policy shown ignores older and equal versions; corrections need the ordering policy discussed below.

sections.heading: 2.3 Bound everything that retains work
sections.text: The ring's fixed capacity limits its entry count. To estimate memory, I also have to account for the values themselves and everything else that retains them: the index, worker mailboxes and batches, encoding buffers, and cache clients. Variable-sized values need a size limit or a byte budget before I can claim a memory bound. In the proposed single-pending-queue design, a rough payload allowance is (C + W * B) * Emax: pending capacity C, W workers, at most B claimed events per worker, and maximum retained event size Emax. Index and client overhead need their own allowances. The existing implementation also has copies and extra channels, so this expression does not bound its memory usage. A small worker pool limits simultaneous application-level writes if each worker waits for its write to finish. Counting client objects gives no such assurance, since a client may manage several connections. And without write deadlines, a stalled cache can leave every worker occupied indefinitely. Batch size and the flush deadline let me trade waiting time for less network overhead. Here too, the implementation needs a closer look: the writer collects a batch, but the storage adapter executes its pipeline separately for each event. Changing the batch size will not give it one network execution per batch.

sections.heading: 2.4 Preserve ordering at the final write
sections.text: A writer can claim a temperature reading just before a newer one arrives. Another writer may claim the newer reading and finish first. If both writes are unconditional, the older reading then overwrites it. Coalescing while observations are pending does not protect them once they are in flight. The current dispatcher assigns work round-robin, so updates for a key can reach different workers even if they arrived in partition order. Its cache writes are unconditional. The registry's timestamp comparison cannot prevent this later overwrite. The cache needs to apply the same rule: replace a metric only when the incoming version is newer. With concurrent writers, comparison and replacement must be atomic. Reading the version in a client and then writing leaves room for another writer to act between the two operations. A cache-side conditional update can close that race. Exclusive ownership of a key is another option, provided it covers every writer, including recovery. Choosing a version also commits us to an ordering policy. Observation timestamps depend on the devices' clocks and reset behavior; equal timestamps, corrections, and sequence resets need explicit handling. Arrival order will not resolve this when replay or delayed delivery can reorder observations.

sections.heading: 2.5 A dropped final update does not repair itself
sections.text: I left retries out of the initial proposal because a later reading could replace a lost one. For a frequently reporting metric, that may be an acceptable delay. But it assumes that another reading arrives and its write succeeds. If the device goes offline instead, its last update may remain missing. That is where my original claim of eventual consistency needs qualification. To promise eventual recovery of that observation, the system needs replay or reconciliation. Historical storage can supply the data; something still has to find the missing state and repair it. I also need to know where loss occurs. Ignoring an older observation discards superseded work. Evicting a pending entry or failing a write can lose a value the cache needs. The current path counts outcomes at one boundary, while dispatch can drop silently and the worker discards the returned write error. A single "dropped" counter would hide the distinction even if it counted all of these cases. Meanwhile, event publication remains a separate responsibility. It is not transactional with cache admission: a cache update can succeed even when publication fails. Launching an unbounded goroutine for each publication would also defeat the memory budget. The required path needs its own publication acknowledgement and input-offset handling.

sections.heading: 2.6 What I give up, and where the design stops working
sections.text: The appeal of this design is that cache trouble does not force the processor to retain an ever-growing backlog. Coalescing removes superseded work, while eviction gives the queue a way to stay within capacity. I pay for that with incomplete state and potentially longer delays before a device's next reading reaches the cache. Avoiding retries keeps the write path simple, but leaves recovery to later observations or a separate repair mechanism. A process that stays alive through overload has met only part of the requirement. Its cache can still be too stale to use.

sections.heading: 2.6.1 When there is little work to coalesce
sections.text: Repeated temperature updates for one device are cheap to hold: they share one pending slot. The same number of updates spread over different devices and metrics may each need a slot and a write. Event rate alone therefore says little about how much this design saves. If the writes required to keep those metrics within the chosen freshness target exceed the cache's sustained capacity, no finite buffer can meet that target indefinitely. A larger ring buys time during a burst. Under sustained overload, it can retain more work while the view continues to fall behind. Shedding may keep the service running, but it cannot preserve the promised freshness and coverage at the same time. The eviction policy also makes no promise to each device. Enough new identities can displace a rarely reporting metric before a writer claims it. If its device then stays quiet, frequent updates elsewhere do nothing to repair that missing value. A single hot key cannot fill this deduplicating queue on its own; competition comes from the number of different keys needing service. There are two memory limits to consider as well. The pending queue must fit in the processor, and the retained current-state dataset must fit in the cache. Bounding the queue does not bound the number of devices and metrics stored over time. If that dataset exceeds available cache memory, capacity or retention has to change. Otherwise writes can fail or stored entries may be evicted, depending on the cache policy, independently of the pending queue's behavior.

sections.heading: 2.6.2 When best effort becomes a broken promise
sections.text: This design is a poor fit when every observation matters, or when every device must appear in the view within a fixed deadline despite failures. Eviction and unretried write failures explicitly allow those requirements to be violated. A larger buffer cannot change the delivery contract. Even for a current-state view, accepting occasional loss is a stronger choice for a metric that reports rarely than for one that reports frequently. I would need repair if the last reading before a device goes offline must eventually appear. If the source no longer retains that observation, or no recovery path can read it, the cache cannot reconstruct it. Version checks depend on trustworthy ordering too. With timestamps as versions, one erroneous future timestamp can cause subsequent normal readings to be rejected until they overtake it. Atomic comparison would faithfully enforce the wrong order. Clock validation or a suitable version and correction policy has to resolve that; coalescing cannot.

sections.heading: 2.6.3 When cache trouble spreads to the primary path
sections.text: The secondary path shares a process with required publication. It still spends CPU on each offered event, takes the queue lock, and allocates or encodes data. A bounded queue limits retained work, not the cost of an unlimited stream of admission attempts. If that work exhausts shared CPU or creates enough memory pressure, publication can slow down even though admission never waits for cache capacity. Fixed workers and byte limits reduce the risk; separate resource budgets, and eventually process isolation, may be needed for a stronger boundary. Recovery can spread the load in the other direction. If cache misses make readers query history, an outage can move the read workload onto the historical store. If replay then competes with live writes at full speed, recovery can overload the cache again. Google's Addressing Cascading Failures describes how shifting load after a failure can exhaust the remaining capacity. Fallback and repair need admission limits of their own. Repair given only spare capacity will never catch up while live work consumes the entire write budget. I would use this approach for a replaceable current-state projection whose readers tolerate visible gaps or delay, with enough normal capacity to recover after bursts. If the requirement becomes complete, deadline-bound delivery for every metric, I would need durable pending work or replay, flow control, and capacity sized for that requirement. The bounded ring would still be useful as a local optimization, but it would no longer be the delivery mechanism.

sections.heading: 3 How I would evolve the system
sections.text: Once the cache branch stays within its resource budget, I still need to decide whether the view it produces is useful. How stale or incomplete may it become? That requirement should guide further changes.

sections.heading: 3.1 Start with the freshness readers need
sections.text: Queue occupancy alone would tell me too little. I would also track the oldest pending work, the delay until a successful write, and the reasons updates are lost. Observation age needs separate attention: a quiet device can have an old reading while ingestion is healthy. Broker lag helps distinguish that case from a processor that has fallen behind. A queue full of repeated updates for a few metrics is a good candidate for coalescing. If most entries belong to different metrics, that will buy less; admission or capacity needs to change. Slow writes while little work is pending call for a different investigation again. A larger queue can make the screen staler without speeding up any of those writes. I would measure retained bytes and write cost alongside events per second. Google's Handling Overload discusses the limits of request-count capacity models and the value of treating work differently according to its criticality. Here, required publication and a replaceable cache projection already have different delivery requirements.

sections.heading: 3.2 Give repair a budget
sections.text: After bounding the write path and enforcing ordering, I would add a repair path that can identify stale or missing state and recover it from the source. Recovery needs a rate limit too. Replaying everything at full speed after an outage can overload the cache just as it becomes available again. Live updates and repair could share a write budget, with repair using spare capacity. The version rule must apply to both, so a delayed historical read cannot overwrite a newer observation. When the freshness target cannot be met within that budget, the service should report that the view is degraded. A normal shutdown can leave missing work as well. I would stop admission and join the producers, then drain accepted work within a deadline before closing the clients. Anything left needs to be counted and covered by repair. A fixed sleep cannot tell me whether the writers have finished.

sections.heading: 3.3 Scale the constrained part
sections.text: More workers can help while the cache has spare write capacity. Beyond that, they increase contention or move the wait into connection pools. Partitioning the pending queue would bring ownership and rebalancing into the ordering design. If a noisy source repeatedly crowds out rarely reporting devices, separate allowances may be needed to protect their pending updates. I would wait for evidence of those problems before adding the machinery. The delivery and ordering gaps need fixing first; tuning an adaptive concurrency controller would be difficult while write errors and missing updates were still indistinguishable. I would test this with the cache unavailable, checking that publication continues within its own admission limits and pending cache work stays bounded. During recovery, readers must still be able to tell when their view is behind, while repair catches up without displacing live traffic. Until that behavior is established, I would describe the projection as best effort rather than promise eventual consistency.

documents.title: From Time-Series to State: Designing a Cache for Periodic Device Telemetry

sections.text: A table of device readings was slow during ordinary use. Each request looked up the latest observations, assembled the devices, and serialized the result. The next request repeated much of that work, even when few readings had changed. The proposed design stores each device as a hash of independently encoded metrics. An update replaces one field; a selective read decodes only the fields it needs. Assembled JSON has a separate place in the design: a short-lived local snapshot. Snapshot reuse and permission to query history are separate choices. 1 A slow view of current readings 2 The devices give us some room 3 Maintain what the table keeps asking for 4 Store metrics in the shape they arrive 4.1 Follow two metrics through the hash 5 Give updates a short window to meet 6 A fast lookup can still make a slow response 7 How fresh does this request need to be? 8 When the live state stops moving 9 Where the work belongs 10 References

sections.heading: 1 A slow view of current readings
sections.text: The table needed current readings from many devices. Behind it, the backend queried a time-series store for the most recent values of each metric, combined them into device-level structures, and returned the result. Work that was manageable for one device became expensive across a larger view. There was a reasonable explanation for every step. The observations lived in a time-series database, the table needed their latest values, and the backend assembled the response the client expected. Taken together, those steps made ordinary use painfully slow. The incoming data offers a smaller unit of work. Each observation changes one metric, while the table asks for an assembled view of many metrics. Keeping those two representations separate lets the update path stay small without making every reader reconstruct devices from history.

sections.heading: 2 The devices give us some room
sections.text: Consider physical meters, sensors, and controllers that report measurements periodically. A table of their latest observations does not necessarily need a reaction within milliseconds. The acceptable delay depends on what the view is used for. Each metric also arrives independently. A temperature observation may be newer than the last consumption reading. There is no single message containing the complete, current device. The table therefore needs the latest known observation for each metric. Those observations may have different ages. Keeping their timestamps matters: a newly assembled response must not make an old reading look newly measured. This leaves room to maintain the device's state between requests, and to reuse an assembled response briefly when the caller allows it.

sections.heading: 3 Maintain what the table keeps asking for
sections.text: The design adds a current-state projection alongside historical storage. As telemetry arrives, a consumer updates the latest metric values in a shared cache. The time-series store remains the historical source; the projection serves the recurring current-state lookup. For each device and metric, the merge rule is small: The per-metric merge rule, shown as pseudocode. if no value is stored, or incoming.timestamp > stored.timestamp: store incoming value and timestamp Under that rule, an older observation arriving late cannot replace a newer stored one. Different metrics can advance independently, so an out-of-order temperature update need not prevent a consumption update from being applied. The comparison and replacement need to happen atomically. Reading a timestamp and writing the value in separate operations would let concurrent updates overwrite one another. The timestamp must also be a meaningful ordering key; the rule cannot correct a wrongly timestamped observation. Figure 1: Conceptual update and read paths. The service can reuse local snapshots or load shared metric state. Historical queries for missing devices are separately controlled; a snapshot-only request uses neither backend. Historical ingestion is omitted. The state is an aggregate of observations, not a measurement of the whole device at one instant. That fits the table's purpose without pretending the devices report more synchronously than they do.

sections.heading: 4 Store metrics in the shape they arrive
sections.text: One option is a serialized JSON object for each device. That resembles the response, but changing a single metric means rewriting the object. Reading a subset also means deserializing unrelated values. The proposed layout uses one hash per device, with independently addressable metric fields [1]. Each field holds a compact byte string containing its timestamp, value, and optional unit. The cache selects the field; the application decodes what is inside it. Figure 2: One device hash maps metric names to individual byte strings. The expanded field shows fixed-width timestamp and length fields followed by variable-length UTF-8 contents. The illustrative temperature payload occupies 18 bytes; cell widths are schematic, and hash keys and storage overhead are excluded. Both text fields use the same decoding rule: read the length, then consume that many bytes. A missing unit has length zero and needs no separate parsing path. Although the decoder could infer the unit's length from the remaining buffer, the explicit length keeps it independent of that outer boundary and makes each metric payload self-delimiting, at a cost of one byte per metric. Values remain text in this representation; interpreting a reading as a number or another type is the reader's job. The fixed fields occupy 11 bytes: 8 for the timestamp in Unix milliseconds, 2 for the value's byte length, and 1 for the unit's byte length. The payload then needs as many bytes as the UTF-8 value and unit contain. In the example, the value 21.4 takes 4 bytes and the unit °C takes 3, giving 18 bytes (144 bits) in total. That counts the metric payload, not the field name, device key, or storage engine's overhead. A new voltage reading can then update voltage without reconstructing temperature and consumption. The service can also ask for the fields a particular view needs. Those selected fields still need decoding, but the others can remain untouched. The JSON response becomes something built from that state, rather than the unit that every update must replace.

sections.heading: 4.1 Follow two metrics through the hash
sections.text: Consider an initially empty hash for a fictional device. The timestamps below are ordered t0 < t1 < t2 < t3; arrival order differs from observation order. Arrival Metric Timestamp Reading Effect First temperature t1 21.4 °C Store the temperature field Next voltage t2 3.5 V Store voltage; leave temperature at t1 Late temperature t0 20.9 °C Ignore it; the stored temperature is newer Latest temperature t3 21.8 °C Replace temperature; leave voltage at t2 A temperature-only read now selects that field and decodes 21.8 °C with timestamp t3. It does not fetch or decode voltage. A view needing both metrics can select both, retaining their different timestamps. Neither read needs to replay the arrivals to discover which values survived. This example describes the storage layout's capabilities. A public API can choose a coarser boundary, such as returning all metrics for the selected devices; field-level storage does not require field selection in every endpoint.

sections.heading: 5 Give updates a short window to meet
sections.text: Field-level updates remove the full-object rewrite. Issuing a separate request for every incoming metric would still create substantial network overhead under load. The consumer can briefly collect updates for each device, merge them, and write them together. The window should be small relative to the delay the application can accept. If the same metric appears more than once in the window, the newest timestamp wins there too. The stored state still needs its own atomic comparison when the batch is applied. There is no need to wait for unrelated devices. One device's updates can be flushed while another device's window is still open. The small delay buys fewer network round trips, which is a useful trade for readings that normally arrive seconds or minutes apart.

sections.heading: 6 A fast lookup can still make a slow response
sections.text: Once the state is cheap to read, the table still needs a response containing many devices. Fetching fields from the cache does not remove the CPU work of turning them into JSON. For repeated reads of one device, a short-lived JSON snapshot local to the read service can avoid rebuilding the same response. A request spanning many devices also needs efficient assembly: collect the selected fields into a shared buffer, reuse memory where practical, and reuse per-device snapshots when they fit the request. This gives the two cache representations different jobs. Metric fields are convenient to update and select. Serialized snapshots are convenient to return. Using both avoids making every update pay for a response that nobody may read, or making every reader assemble a response that was just assembled.

sections.heading: 7 How fresh does this request need to be?
sections.text: A routine table read can reuse unexpired local snapshots and load the devices missing from them. Those snapshots expire after a configured lifetime. If a reader wants a newly assembled response, it can skip existing snapshots and replace them with the loaded result. Another request can skip snapshot reads and writes altogether, leaving the local cache undisturbed. A snapshot-only read makes a different trade-off: it returns what is available locally without contacting either backend. That can mean a partial result, or an empty one when none of the requested devices are available. It does not start rebuilding the missing snapshots. Permission to query history is a separate choice. A table refresh can still read shared metric state while avoiding the cost of historical queries for missing devices. An existing snapshot may contain data obtained by an earlier historical lookup; disabling that lookup for this request does not change where an already cached result came from. There are two ages here. Snapshot age describes when the response was assembled. Observation age describes when the device produced a reading. A snapshot built now may contain a consumption value from several minutes ago. Expiring the snapshot does not make that measurement newer, and an old metric timestamp does not by itself trigger a historical query. The caller must judge the reading's age separately from the lifetime of its JSON representation. For a view that can accept a short delay, snapshot reuse avoids repeated assembly between device reports. A view of both metrics might reuse a device snapshot made before t3 while that snapshot remains unexpired. Skipping it would load the current metric state instead. Whether missing devices also trigger historical queries depends on the separate lookup policy.

sections.heading: 8 When the live state stops moving
sections.text: When a requested device is missing from shared metric state, the service can query history if the request allows it. The assembled result can enter the local snapshot cache when the snapshot policy permits. A request restricted to local snapshots never reaches this path. Without historical lookups, missing devices are omitted from the result. A failure to reach the shared cache is still an error, not proof that the devices have no readings. Keeping those cases separate prevents a backend outage from looking like a successful but empty table. If the consumer stops, cached readings stop advancing. Catching up requires retained events or reconstruction from history, including updates that were buffered but not written before the consumer exited. The merge rule still applies during recovery: a delayed rebuild must not replace a newer value already received from the stream. Observation timestamps help readers judge the result's age, but the service also needs to distinguish a quiet device from an ingestion path that has stopped receiving updates.

sections.heading: 9 Where the work belongs
sections.text: Historical storage remains useful for history and recovery. The proposed read path serves the usual request from maintained metric state, with short-lived local snapshots avoiding repeated assembly. Readers can control snapshot reuse without automatically enabling expensive historical lookups. The changes follow the work that was being repeated. Per-metric state avoids reconstructing devices from history. Short, per-device batches reduce write overhead. Response snapshots avoid assembling the same JSON for every reader. This is a useful pattern for periodic telemetry because the reporting intervals leave room for those trade-offs. Its suitability comes from what the screen needs to show, how observations arrive, and how much delay the caller can accept. Those decisions can be considered independently of the database products.

sections.heading: 10 References
sections.text: Redis, Redis hashes, a public example of field-addressable storage, not a statement of the deployed technology.

An order API can pass every test while a downstream consumer drops the customer's delivery choice. When several teams own the path from request to result, their pipelines need a way to test that path together. An illustrative express-order change shows how shared container-delivery jobs and a small, scenario-based test setup can support that work, while teams keep their own build tools and checks. A passing result is useful for deployment only while it still describes the combination being deployed. 1 One change, several teams 2 Start with the behavior 3 What the test pyramid leaves to the pipeline 3.1 Alternatives and their limits 4 Build the part of the platform you need 4.1 Optional implementation with spex 5 Reuse delivery jobs across applications 6 Know what a passing test covered 6.1 If deployment approval uses a shared target 6.2 Keep reports tied to the image 7 Deploy the combination that was checked 7.1 Roll out and recover the express-order change 8 Keep the shared setup worth maintaining 9 References

sections.heading: 1 One change, several teams
sections.text: Suppose we add express delivery to an order-processing application. The order API validates the request and publishes an acceptance event. A consumer updates a query model, and the application displays the accepted order. To the customer, this is one operation. Its implementation may belong to several teams. The API team can add the new field and pass its tests while a downstream consumer silently drops it. Even a small change therefore raises a question that no single team's build can answer: does the delivery option survive the whole trip? Those teams may use different repositories and build tools. Some services sit behind private networks or in separate infrastructure accounts. Requiring everyone to adopt one pipeline or deploy together would make a local change depend on a much larger reorganization. The approach here shares the recurring image-delivery work and gives teams a repeatable way to check behavior across their boundaries. It uses GitHub Actions, Helm, and Kubernetes; older systems can remain dependencies with their own deployment procedures. The order change is an illustrative example, not a report of a company deployment.

sections.heading: 2 Start with the behavior
sections.text: Before changing the pipeline, the API and consumer teams agree what accepting an express order means. The acceptance event must retain the delivery option, and the query must show the accepted order before an agreed deadline. Figure 1: The illustrative order system. The API publishes the delivery option through the event stream; the consumer preserves it in the query model. The scenario follows one order across that path and checks the query result before the agreed deadline. Dashed links represent query and response exchanges. That agreement can become a scenario kept beside the code or in a shared testbench repository: Illustrative express-order behavior with project-defined tags. @domain-orders @capability-order-acceptance @usecase-express-delivery Feature: Order delivery options Scenario: An accepted order retains its delivery option Given a unique order reference and a valid customer for this test run When the client submits an order with delivery option "express" Then its acceptance event contains delivery option "express" And its query shows "accepted" with "express" delivery before the deadline The test follows one unique order reference from submission to the query result. It waits for asynchronous processing, with the deadline measured from submission. Yesterday's accepted order cannot satisfy it. This gives the teams a concrete behavior to discuss during review. If duplicate events are also part of the requirement, they need a replay scenario as well; this one checks the first accepted result.

sections.heading: 3 What the test pyramid leaves to the pipeline
sections.text: The test pyramid still applies [1]. Request validation belongs in fast unit tests. Integration tests exercise the broker or database, and contracts check what producers and consumers expect at a boundary. The order scenario adds a check of the path those smaller tests cannot establish on their own. Running it across repositories takes some coordination. Someone has to select the service versions, make them available to the test, and retain enough of the result for another team's deployment job to use. Teams must also agree what counts as done; Scrum makes that a shared responsibility for teams working on one product [2]. The pipeline makes their checks repeatable.

sections.heading: 3.1 Alternatives and their limits
sections.text: Mocks and interface specifications remain useful. OpenAPI and AsyncAPI describe HTTP and message contracts [3, 4], but neither establishes that a real consumer preserves the express option through to the query. Maintaining a mock image of every service would also mean maintaining a second implementation of much of the system. At the other extreme, starting the entire platform for each change brings in services that have nothing to do with the order. A shared environment avoids some setup work, but other teams can change it underneath the test. When cross-service changes are rare, a few hand-written journey tests may be enough. A maintained testbench becomes worthwhile when teams repeatedly reconstruct the same setup.

sections.heading: 4 Build the part of the platform you need
sections.text: The express-order scenario needs the API, event stream, consumer, and query service with its store. Authentication or customer services join that setup only if the request depends on them. The rest of the platform can stay out. This is the test slice: the scenario together with the services, configuration, and data needed to exercise it. Teams maintain that setup explicitly. Tags can group scenarios by domain, capability, or use case, but selecting a tag does not discover dependencies or assemble an environment. The smaller setup makes the behavior easier to investigate. If the delivery option disappears, the engineer can follow the request through a manageable set of services. It still needs real dependencies where their behavior matters; a fixture returning a convenient response cannot establish what the actual service will return.

sections.heading: 4.1 Optional implementation with spex
sections.text: One implementation uses spex to translate constrained scenarios into Kubernetes Test TooL (KUTTL) workspaces [8]. Teams maintain a catalog of supported operations, so a readable step still needs an implementation behind it. Scenario selection and environment setup remain separate [9]. A suite chooses the scenarios; profiles describe the services to install, and bindings identify the endpoints to call. The order profile brings up the participating services with the candidate API image and pinned companion versions. A replay check might use a smaller setup without the API. The same arrangement can run locally in a temporary Kind cluster [10] or against existing development services. Shared targets need additional care, as discussed below.

sections.heading: 5 Reuse delivery jobs across applications
sections.text: With the behavior defined, the API team's repository can call a reusable GitHub Actions workflow [5]. Compilation stays in the team's Dockerfile, and the team supplies its test commands. The shared jobs handle the image's journey between build, test, publication, and deployment. The workflow first builds an image or reuses one whose declared build inputs have not changed. It passes an exported image archive and checksum between runners, so test jobs use the selected image rather than build another one. Publication waits for every enabled check to pass. A later release copies the published image to the destination registry and verifies its digest without rebuilding it. Figure 2 follows that image through build and release. Reusing an image saves a build; it does not excuse running the required tests. It also depends on declaring the inputs correctly and refreshing mutable base images or external dependencies when needed. Figure 2: Follow the checksummed image handoff through gated publication and promotion; conditional checks support deployment decisions. Keeping policy separate from build identity matters in small ways too. A pull request once failed before building because a release-branch naming rule was applied to its feature branch. We changed the check to validate the target branch while keeping the source commit as the build identity. Developers could use ordinary feature names without weakening the release policy. Access follows the job's needs. An isolated build need not reach private services; the order test may need an approved runner and scoped credentials. GitHub OpenID Connect can supply short-lived cloud credentials [6], but the platform still has to decide which jobs may use them. Untrusted changes must not gain private access, and permission to test is separate from permission to deploy [7].

sections.heading: 6 Know what a passing test covered
sections.text: Suppose the scenario passes. The event retained express delivery and the query returned the accepted order before the deadline. That result describes the API, consumer, and settings used in that run. The pipeline keeps those versions and settings with the test reports and image identity. The record needs to describe what actually ran, not merely what a job intended to install. Otherwise, the next team cannot tell whether the result applies to its proposed deployment.

sections.heading: 6.1 If deployment approval uses a shared target
sections.text: An isolated slice makes that easier. On a shared target, another team might replace the consumer halfway through the test. Passing assertions would then leave us uncertain about which combination worked. If the result will support deployment approval, the platform needs to prevent competing changes for the duration of the run and invalidate the result if relevant deployments or settings change. That control must work across repositories and reject stale workers at the target. A lock checked only by a job cannot stop it from resuming after its permission has expired. These are requirements on the surrounding platform, not guarantees supplied by spex or a reusable workflow. Where target changes cannot be controlled or observed, the result has that limitation. An isolated setup is preferable when the necessary dependencies can be recreated.

sections.heading: 6.2 Keep reports tied to the image
sections.text: Shared jobs retain reports from trusted runs alongside the selected image; spex can supply JUnit results for CI [8]. Deployment jobs need to verify where a report came from rather than trust an arbitrary file claiming success. Captured diagnostics must also leave out credentials. The reports should help the engineer follow a failure. Did the API reject the request? Did the event lose the field? Did the consumer fail to update the query? A wrong endpoint or unavailable broker needs a different fix. The testbench is only useful if it makes those distinctions easier to investigate.

sections.heading: 7 Deploy the combination that was checked
sections.text: Now suppose the API image stays unchanged, but another team releases a new consumer. The earlier passing test no longer answers the same question. For the example below, A2 is the API image digest; C1 and C2 are different consumer image digests. Express delivery remains enabled and the other inputs stay fixed. Stage Combination Decision Recorded pass A2 with C1 Retain coverage of A2/C1 Later proposal A2 with C2 Hold pending coverage of A2/C2 Rolling proposal A2 with C1, C2 Cover both paths and their coexistence A mixed rollout matters too. A test that happens to reach C1 says nothing about the C2 path or their coexistence. Before deployment starts, the release owner needs results that cover the combinations customers can actually encounter. The deployment controls must keep the target consistent with that decision. The test environment need not match production, but the assumptions behind the test must hold in both. For the express-order scenario, that includes compatible event formats, a consumer that preserves the delivery option, and processing that meets the agreed deadline. Where possible, make those assumptions executable checks. Before using the result to approve a rollout, check whether any environment differences could invalidate it. If they could, rerun the affected checks against the proposed setup. Different endpoints or credentials can be expected; they still need to reach the intended services. A changed processing mode or feature flag may alter the behavior itself. An external service that can change without an observable version also limits what an earlier test can establish. The release owner must decide whether a fresh target check is needed or whether to accept the remaining risk explicitly.

sections.heading: 7.1 Roll out and recover the express-order change
sections.text: For this change, the teams can first deploy a consumer that handles existing events and preserves the new field, then introduce the producer that sends it. If old consumers remain active, the new producer must work with them too, or the option must stay disabled until they have left service. Older stored orders and replayed events belong in those compatibility checks. The release coordinator gets agreement on that sequence and how long old formats remain supported. Operators need authority to stop the rollout; someone must also be accountable for resolving disagreements and approving exceptions. An exception records a decision to accept risk, not a passing test. During activation, the operations owner watches the acceptance-to-query delay and consumer backlog against agreed stop conditions. Disabling the option may contain a problem, but orders already accepted still need processing or repair. Redeploying an earlier image cannot undo database writes or recall events. If an express order later appears as standard delivery, the immediate task is recovery. Once the cause is understood, a regression scenario can preserve what the teams learned for the next change.

sections.heading: 8 Keep the shared setup worth maintaining
sections.text: Service teams own the behavior and maintain the scenarios that check it. Workflow maintainers own the shared delivery machinery; platform owners control access and deployment writes. Those roles may overlap, but the responsibilities need to be clear. Figure 3: Responsibilities in the proposed delivery arrangement. Teams contribute behavioral checks, maintainers provide repeatable execution, operators control targets, and release roles coordinate agreements and accountable decisions. Start with shared build and test jobs, then add a slice for a recurring cross-service check. The catalog and setup need maintenance as services change, and generated workspaces must remain readable enough to debug. Versioned workflows also need an upgrade policy that includes their separately referenced actions. Shared targets can become a queue. Adding runners will not help when builds must wait for the same resources; the remedy may be a smaller shared scope or more isolation. Tests also need to leave existing infrastructure intact and clean up only what they created. Judge the shared jobs and the testbench separately. Compare the build and setup work saved with the time spent maintaining and debugging them. If teams spend more time interpreting generated failures than they save in setup, simplify the testbench before adding more scenarios.

A note in Emacs and a page on the web serve different purposes. The useful question is not whether they look identical, but whether the structure, examples, and connections that make the note useful survive the journey. This guide connects two working examples in the notebook. Start with the publishing fixture to inspect individual features, then read the Rust article to see those features supporting an explanation. Inspect the publishing surface Read an example in context Keep the connections in the source Read another author’s workflow Questions to explore next

sections.heading: Inspect the publishing surface
sections.text: The Org-mode publishing showcase deliberately puts headings, tables, task states, inline formatting, and source blocks together. It is the place to look when asking a narrow question: does this part of an Org document still make sense after export? The route here is Org → ox-hugo Markdown → Berlin’s semantic document → HTML. Each stage has a different responsibility. Emacs remains the authoring environment; the published page does not reproduce folding, agendas, or capture workflows. The showcase documents examples, not a promise of support for every Org feature.

sections.heading: Read an example in context
sections.text: Processing JSON with Rust is a learning exercise rather than a publishing test. Read it for the relationship between the prose, the source listings, and the medal results. Code references let an explanation point to a precise part of a listing without turning the whole article into a wall of code. The worked medal pipeline also makes a useful distinction visible: showing the steps of an execution is not the same as executing a program in the reader’s browser. Stored Org results can accompany source code; Berlin’s publishing export does not execute the code blocks again.

sections.heading: Keep the connections in the source
sections.text: The links above are Org ID links. Their targets are document identities, not hand-maintained HTML filenames. Berlin resolves them against the published collection and derives backlinks to the passages that refer to each note. That division keeps two different kinds of organisation separate. Tags gather material with shared labels. A guide chooses a route through that material and explains why each stop belongs. The explanation remains ordinary prose, so it can change as the notebook grows.

sections.heading: Read another author’s workflow
sections.text: Dominik Honnef’s My org-roam workflows for taking notes and writing articles describes a broader system connecting notes, references, and web publication. His use of category notes is especially relevant here: a category can contain an explanation as well as collect links. It offers a useful comparison, not a description of the configuration used by this website.

sections.heading: Questions to explore next
sections.text: These two questions are starting points for further investigation, not completed experiments. Each connects something already in the notebook to a small next step.

sections.heading: What would make a stored result reproducible?
sections.text: The worked example in Processing JSON with Rust places a small input beside its extraction, counting, and ranking results. That makes the explanation inspectable. It does not, by itself, establish that another environment will produce the same result. The uncertainty is what needs to accompany the stored output: the exact input, source listings, dependency lockfile, Rust toolchain, and execution command are a starting point. Is that enough to reproduce this particular example? A small experiment would be to use a disposable copy of the example, record those inputs, and compare a fresh execution with the stored table. Then change one medal in the small input and regenerate the results. Record what changed and whether the explanation still matches. Run this explicitly during authoring; the publishing export should continue to use stored results. The useful follow-up would be a short note containing the recorded setup, comparison, and any mismatch—not a claim of reproducibility before trying it.

sections.heading: Where should a guide end and a note begin?
sections.text: This guide introduces both the publishing showcase and the Rust learning exercise. The uncertainty is how much orientation belongs here without repeating the explanations in those notes. A small reading exercise would be to follow the links with two different questions: “Which Org features can I inspect?” and “How do code references support an explanation?” For each route, record the first place where context is missing or unnecessarily repeated. Put route-finding context in the guide and keep the technical explanation beside its example. The result may be only a revised paragraph or a better link. A separate note is useful when there is an observation worth explaining, not just to fill out the collection.

I write in Emacs Org-mode. This page is where I check what happens to that writing on its way to the web: Org source is exported by ox-hugo to Markdown, then parsed and rendered by Berlin. It is both a public example and a publishing fixture. The deliberately deep headings, task states, tables, and code blocks give me a varied document to inspect when I change the pipeline. This is not a claim of complete Org-mode support; it is a place to make the current behavior visible. What to look for This is an example headline Another headline Basic markup Showing and hiding headlines Tables Org-mode links Various things you can add in headers The TODO-planner payoff Exporting an org-mode buffer Further authoring features and source blocks

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.text: Structure: nested headings and lists should remain understandable outside Emacs, including where the exporter turns deep outlines into lists. Inline content: emphasis, verbatim text, and links should preserve their meaning and remain readable. Tables and tasks: compare the table layout, checkboxes, task labels, tags, and priority markers in the examples below. Code and stored results: source blocks should be readable as listings. Publishing does not execute them; any displayed results are already present in the Org source. Folding, agenda views, capture commands, and keyboard shortcuts belong to the Emacs authoring experience. Describing them here does not make them interactive features of this static page. Some export-specific material, such as LaTeX, may need additional handling rather than appearing exactly as it does in Emacs. The examples below were retained from an introductory document described as the example file for a Denver Emacs Org-mode talk. They remain useful as a varied publishing fixture; the talk-oriented examples are not a description of my personal setup. For these publishing features in a regular article, see Processing JSON with Rust. That link also exercises the resolution of an Org ID into a published page.

sections.heading: Basic markup
sections.text: You can really go as deep as you want. This is the general building block for org-mode navigation. Next, let's talk about some markup underscores let you underline things stars add emphasis slashes are italics pluses are strikethrough equal signs are verbatim text tildes can also be used You can generate lists with the - character (seen above), or create numbered ones: Number one thing Number two thing Number three

sections.heading: Showing and hiding headlines
sections.text: You can hide the contents of a headline by putting the point (cursor) or it and hitting TAB. You can also toggle hiding and showing of all headlines with SHIFT-TAB.

sections.heading: Tables
sections.text: Auto expanding tables are one of the coolest features of org-mode, because tables in Markdown just plain suck. In order to create a new table, you can start typing it manually, or press C-c |, which will prompt for the table's dimensions. First Name Last Name Years using Emacs Lee Hinman 5 Mike Hunsinger 2 Daniel Glauser 4 Really-long-first-name-guy long-last-name-pers 1

sections.heading: Org-mode links
sections.text: :PROPERTIES:... In an org-mode file, you can press C-c l to store a pointer to wherever you are in the file. Then, with (or without) text highlighted hit C-C C-l to make it into a link. The example file for Magit If you don't want to store a pointer (ie, link to a website or something), you can just hit C-c C-l and type or paste the link. To manually create a link, do something like: The Denver Emacs Meetup Group Writequit site Google's web site Google (ignore the *_SRC blocks for now, we'll get there) [[http://google.com/][Google]] You can link to files, images, websites, emails, irc, and all kinds of things.

sections.heading: Various things you can add in headers
sections.text: One of the most common uses for org-mode is a sort of "task list" or TODO list. Org-mode supports this by allowing markers in the headline for the state of a task. Let's look at an example:

sections.heading: TODO This is a task that needs doing
TODO Another todo task
sections.text: sub task one sub task two sub task three

sections.heading: TODO learn other stuff
sections.text: You can toggle each task in a list with the C-c C-c keyboard shortcut.

sections.heading: DONE I've already finished this one
sections.text: You can change the status of a task by hitting C-c t in the body of a task anywhere, which will prompt for the state to put it in. You can create as many of these as you'd like, for example (from my own config, use what works best for you, configuring them is a little out of scope right here) here's what I use:

sections.heading: WAITING waiting for someone else before doing anything
NEEDSREVIEW there's a PR for this, it needs someone to look at it
HOLD this is in permanent hold until further notice
CANCELLED I don't need this any more
SOMEDAY I'd like to do this someday in the waaaaay off future
sections.text: A lot of people just use "TODO" and "DONE" though.

sections.heading: The TODO-planner payoff
sections.text: :PROPERTIES:... So TODOs are all well and good, but what is a really neat feature is when you can easily capture new TODOs and display them easily. In order to do this, let's configure a couple of Emacs options in your emacs init: (require 'org) ;; Setup C-c c to capture new TODOs (global-set-key (kbd "C-c c") 'org-capture) ;; Setup a key bind for the agenda (global-set-key (kbd "C-c a") 'org-agenda) ;; Set up agenda to know about our file, you can use a list of files or ;; directories here (setq org-agenda-files '("~/todo.org")) ;; A new template (setq org-capture-templates '(("t" "Todo" entry (file "~/todo.org") "* TODO %?\n%U\n"))) Now, hit C-c c to bring up the capture template list, then t to capture a new TODO item. Once you've captured a few TODOs, you can try out the agenda by hitting C-c a, which will prompt for what agenda you'd like to see, for now hit t to see the TODO list agenda.

sections.heading: Exporting an org-mode buffer
sections.text: Org has a lot of export options, they are all contained behind a C-c C-e export backend, exporting to HTML, markdown, plain text, pdf, etc.

sections.heading: Further authoring features and source blocks
sections.text: Org-mode also supports the following authoring workflows. They are listed for context, not as features implemented by this website: refiling (org-refile) source code blocks org-babel clocking in/out table formulas custom agenda views capturing notes (not just TODOs) publishing projects remotely via TRAMP The remaining examples exercise export of LaTeX, Emacs Lisp and shell source blocks, and stored results. They are display examples, not instructions to run the shell commands below. a + b (defun my/function () "docstring" (interactive) (progn (+ 1 1) (message "Hi"))) echo $data > /tmp/foo for i in `cat /tmp/foo`; do echo $i done echo "hi" # do some things echo "stuff" echo "more stuff" echo <<hi>> To enter and edit a block of text, use C-c C-'

As I’ve been learning Rust, I’ve been looking for easy and practical projects to get my head around basic concepts and increase my syntax muscle memory. One of the more common tasks is to load data from different sources, like text files, or more structured data like JSON. So it got me thinking, how would parsing a fairly complex JSON look like in Rust? Luckily, it is not this difficult! The code Let's add indexing operations Conclusion Next Steps This post is a demonstration of using serde_json to parse JSON in Rust. For this purpose, I am using the athletics data set of the Olympic Games Tokyo 2020. The goal is to find the five most successful countries and print them. Print the top five countries and the medals they won. United States of America MedalCount { g: 7, s: 12, b: 7 } Italy MedalCount { g: 5, s: 0, b: 0 } Kenya MedalCount { g: 4, s: 4, b: 2 } Poland MedalCount { g: 4, s: 2, b: 3 } Jamaica MedalCount { g: 4, s: 1, b: 4 } Org-mode publishing showcase I chose an excerpt of the athletics data set, because its a bit more complex than a typical hello world example. The data set is deeply nested, contains a lot of data and different object types and to make things even more interesting some data, such as the countryObject field appears to be inconsistent. Figure 1: Structure of our JSON data The expanded path runs through pageProps, gameDiscipline, events, awards, and participant to countryObject. Open the full-size JSON tree In order to print the requested information, we need to parse the JSON data and extract the fields medalType and the countryObejct as shown above. A detail in the data countryObject is not always an object. The lookup tests is_object() before choosing the field and otherwise falls back to country. See the country lookup

sections.heading: The code
sections.text: Serde_json allows us to map JSON data to enums and this is what we are going to do. Since we also want to count the different types of medals we define a struct called MedalCount. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize)] enum Class { #[serde(rename = "GOLD")] Gold, #[serde(rename = "SILVER")] Silver, #[serde(rename = "BRONZE")] Bronze, } #[derive(Default, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct MedalCount { g: usize, s: usize, b: usize, }

sections.heading: Let's add indexing operations
sections.text: Thanks to serde_json we can easily map the medal data to our enum. But how can we use this information to our advantage once we want to count how many gold, silver and bronze medals a country won? After all, we would like to keep the actual counting as readable as possible and for this, the mapping logic needs be stored elsewhere. Luckily, Rust offers two traits that can be used for indexing operations: Index and IndexMut. By implementing both traits we can map a variant of our class enum to the respective field in our MedalCount struct as shown below. impl Index<Class> for MedalCount { type Output = usize; fn index(&self, class: Class) -> &Self::Output { match class { Class::Gold => &self.g, Class::Silver => &self.s, Class::Bronze => &self.b, } } } impl IndexMut<Class> for MedalCount { fn index_mut(&mut self, class: Class) -> &mut Self::Output { match class { Class::Gold => &mut self.g, Class::Silver => &mut self.s, Class::Bronze => &mut self.b, } } } As far as I know, serde_json does not support mapping of nested data to struct via some form of dot notation. Luckily, if data is not mapped to a predefined struct than the JSON data can still be deserialized into a Value, which then allows us to get the nested data we want. Follow the three operations in this listing: Extract country names, count medals, and rank the results. fn get_class_country_tuple<'a>(values: &'a Vec<Value>) -> Vec<(Class, String)> { let get_country = |participant: &'a serde_json::Value| -> &'a serde_json::Value { let mut country_key = "countryObject"; if !participant[country_key].is_object() { country_key = "country"; } &participant[country_key]["name"] }; let to_tuple = |v: &'a Value| { let class = serde_json::from_value::<Class>(v["medalType"].to_owned()).unwrap(); let country = get_country(&v["participant"]).as_str().unwrap().to_string(); (class, country) }; values.iter().map(to_tuple).collect() } // returns a projection on the medals per country data pub fn get_medals_per_country(&self) -> Result<Projection, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let to_medal_country_tuple = |v: &serde_json::Value| get_class_country_tuple(v["awards"].as_array().unwrap()); let group_by_country = |mut acc: HashMap<_, _>, x| { let (class, country): (Class, String) = x; // remember the IndexMut trait, we used it here for indexing // If there is no entry for a country yet, we create one and // initialize the medal count to g: 0, s: 0, b: 0. // The fields will be incremented by one based on the indexing // operations defined earlier. // So, the value "Gold" will be deserialized to the enum variant // Class::Gold which will increment the field `g` of teh struct // MedalCount. acc.entry(country).or_insert(MedalCount::default())[class] += 1; acc }; let events = self.0.json["pageProps"]["gameDiscipline"]["events"] .as_array() .unwrap(); let mut medals_per_country = events .into_iter() .flat_map(to_medal_country_tuple) .fold(HashMap::new(), group_by_country) .into_iter() .collect::<Vec<(_, _)>>(); medals_per_country.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1)); Ok(Projection(medals_per_country)) } Extract the country name. The lookup uses countryObject when it is an object, otherwise country. Accumulate the medals. Each country gets a counter; IndexMut selects the gold, silver, or bronze field to increment. Rank the results. The comparison orders by gold first, then silver, then bronze—not by the total medal count. #[derive(Eq, PartialEq)] struct Projection(Vec<(String, MedalCount)>); impl Projection { fn empty() -> Self { Self(vec![]) } fn take(self, n: usize) -> Self { Self(self.0.into_iter().take(n).collect()) } fn get(&self) -> &Vec<(String, MedalCount)> { &self.0 } } Having all the components in place, we can finally implement the logic we wanted: fn load_data() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sekaiser/rust-sample-parse-json/main/athletics.json"; let db = AthleticsDb::from_url(Url::from_str(url)?)?; let mut last_top5 = Projection::empty(); loop { let medals_per_country = db.get_medals_per_country()?; let top5 = medals_per_country.take(5); if top5 != last_top5 { for e in top5.get() { println!("{} {:?}", e.0, e.1); } last_top5 = top5; } thread::sleep(time::Duration::from_secs(2)); } } { "pageProps": {"gameDiscipline": {"events": [ {"awards": [ {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"countryObject":{"name":"Japan"}}}, {"medalType":"SILVER","participant":{"country":{"name":"Italy"}}}, {"medalType":"BRONZE","participant":{"country":{"name":"Italy"}}}, {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"countryObject":{"name":"Japan"}}}, {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"country":{"name":"Kenya"}}} ]} ]}} } Japan → gold Italy → silver Italy → bronze Japan → gold Kenya → gold Japan: gold 2, silver 0, bronze 0 Italy: gold 0, silver 1, bronze 1 Kenya: gold 1, silver 0, bronze 0 1. Japan — 2 gold 2. Kenya — 1 gold 3. Italy — 1 silver, 1 bronze

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This post demonstrates the usage of serde_json in order to parse nested JSON data. The article also briefly covers how to use traits in order to keep the code organized and the logic clean. Serde is very powerful and I encourage people who are interested in Rust to take a look at it.
